outline.chapter_title: Motivation and Overview of Parameter-Efficient Finetuning
outline.description: Introduces the need for efficient adaptation of large foundation models, reviews existing finetuning paradigms, and motivates the study of orthogonal finetuning and its parameter-efficiency challenges.
subtopics: Scaling of foundation models and cost of full pre‑training
Three families of parameter‑efficient adaptation: finetuning, adapters, prompts
Desirable properties of model finetuning – preserving pretrained knowledge
Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT): formulation and existing limitations
Goal of the book: from OFT to a more parameter‑efficient approach

outline.description: Provides the linear‑algebraic background required to understand orthogonal finetuning, including orthogonal matrices, Cayley transform, and spectral properties.
subtopics: Definitions: orthogonal, unitary, skew‑symmetric matrices
Cayley parameterization and its properties
Preservation of pairwise angles and singular values
Spectral norm invariance under orthogonal left‑multiplication
Implications for training stability and generalization

outline.description: Details the original OFT method, its parameterization, block‑diagonal variant, and empirical strengths and weaknesses.
subtopics: OFT objective and forward‑pass modification
Block‑diagonal orthogonal matrices: construction and parameter count
Zero‑initialization via identity and training dynamics
Empirical advantages over low‑rank methods (e.g., LoRA)
Analysis of expressivity loss due to block sparsity

outline.chapter_title: Information Transmission Perspective on Matrix Factorization
outline.description: Introduces a graph‑theoretic view of composing dense orthogonal matrices from sparse factors, establishing desiderata for parameter efficiency.
subtopics: Dense orthogonal matrices as full bipartite connectivity
Factorizing a matrix into a product of sparse matrices
Grid‑structured graph representation of the factorization
Desiderata: dense connectivity and minimum free edges
Comparison of naive dense factorization vs. structured sparse factorizations

outline.chapter_title: Butterfly Structures and Fast Fourier Transform
outline.description: Explains the Cooley‑Tukey FFT butterfly graph, its sparsity pattern, and why it is an optimal information‑transmission topology.
subtopics: Recursive FFT decomposition and butterfly diagram
Butterfly factor definition and block‑diagonal composition
Properties: O(d log d) edges, full connectivity, invertibility
Historical uses of butterfly matrices in numerical linear algebra

outline.description: Derives the BOFT method by embedding orthogonal butterfly factorizations into OFT, detailing construction, parameter counting, and initialization.
subtopics: Recursive definition of butterfly matrices B(d)
Block‑butterfly components  ~B⁽ᵇ⁾(d,k) and orthogonal constraints
Parameter budget: O(d log d) versus O(d²) and O(bd)
Special cases: BOFT(1,b) = block‑diagonal OFT, BOFT(log d,2) = full dense orthogonal
Zero‑initialization using identity blocks via Cayley transform

outline.description: Covers practical aspects of optimizing BOFT, including multiplicative dropout, learning‑rate schedules, and computational overhead considerations.
subtopics: Multiplicative dropout design for product of orthogonal factors
Gradient flow through multiple sparse orthogonal layers
Runtime analysis: extra matrix multiplications vs. inference cost
Implementation tips: exploiting block sparsity on GPUs/TPUs
Integration with existing PEFT libraries

outline.description: Analyzes the representational power of BOFT, presents key theorems, and discusses trade‑offs between expressivity, regularity, and generalization.
subtopics: Theorem: BOFT is strictly more expressive than block‑diagonal OFT
Approximation of arbitrary orthogonal matrices with butterfly products
Kaleidoscope hierarchy and universal approximation of O(d)
Expressivity vs. over‑parameterization: why full finetuning can fail
Spectral properties and preservation of singular values

outline.description: Positions BOFT within the broader landscape of PEFT methods, comparing to low‑rank (LoRA), adapters, and prompt tuning.
subtopics: Low‑rank reparameterization vs. sparse orthogonal factorization
Inductive bias introduced by butterfly structure versus adapters
Hybrid schemes: combining BOFT with LoRA or adapters
Memory and compute trade‑offs across methods

outline.description: Summarizes experimental results applying BOFT to vision transformers, large language models, and text‑to‑image diffusion models, illustrating its generality.
subtopics: Setup: datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics
Vision tasks: image classification, detection, segmentation
Language tasks: downstream NLU benchmarks, instruction tuning
Diffusion models: controllable image generation
Ablation studies: block size b, number of factors m, dropout rates
Runtime and parameter‑efficiency analysis

outline.description: Provides actionable advice for researchers and engineers to adopt BOFT in real projects.
subtopics: Choosing block size and number of butterfly factors
When to prefer BOFT over LoRA or adapters
Debugging tips: monitoring orthogonality and training stability
Deploying the trained model: folding orthogonal matrices into pretrained weights
Compatibility with quantization and model compression

outline.description: Discusses limitations of BOFT and explores research avenues such as alternative network topologies, runtime optimization, and theoretical extensions.
subtopics: Reducing training overhead of multiple sparse multiplications
Exploring other information‑transmission graphs (e.g., expander graphs)
Learning the sparsity pattern jointly with orthogonal factors
Extending BOFT to convolutional kernels and attention matrices
Potential for unsupervised or continual learning scenarios
